issues.legal_issue: Selling trees of spontaneous growth does not make their owner a dealer as a seller of goods produced by that person when the owner has made no effort or employed no process to bring the trees into existence.
material_facts: The company sold trees of spontaneous growth from its private forest.
It had not planted the trees or otherwise done anything towards their production.
The company did not cut or uproot the trees; the contractor performed the cutting.
The Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal found that no process had been employed by the company to produce timber.
issues.conclusion: The company was not a dealer under section 2(viii) of the Kerala General Sales Tax Act, 1963, because it had not produced the trees it sold.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(viii) includes a person who sells goods produced by that person by manufacture, agriculture, horticulture or otherwise. In this context, “produced” requires volition and effort involving a process that brings goods into existence; the word “otherwise” does not dispense with that requirement. The Court referred to definitions of “produce” in the Shorter Oxford English Dictionary and Webster’s International English Dictionary and relied on no earlier cases.

issues.legal_issue: Sales of trees that the seller did not produce are not taxable under the Act on the ground that the seller is a dealer selling goods produced by that seller.
material_facts: The company sold trees of spontaneous growth from its private forest.
It had not planted the trees or otherwise done anything towards their production.
The company did not cut or uproot the trees; the contractor performed the cutting.
The assessing authority treated the sale proceeds as taxable turnover, but the Tribunal held that the company was not a dealer.
issues.conclusion: The company was not liable to sales tax on these sales on the basis that it was a dealer selling goods produced by it; the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 2(viii) of the Kerala General Sales Tax Act, 1963, the relevant inclusion covers a person who sells goods produced by that person by manufacture, agriculture, horticulture or otherwise. Spontaneous growth without the seller’s effort or an employed process does not amount to production by the seller. The Court referred to dictionary definitions of “produce” and relied on no earlier cases.
